sections.heading: Overview
sections.content:
The Overhead Carry with Kettlebell is a single-arm loaded carry where the lifter walks a set distance while holding a kettlebell directly overhead with one arm fully extended.

It builds shoulder stability, scapular control, and full-body bracing under an asymmetrical load.

The offset bell of the kettlebell adds a unique stability challenge compared to a dumbbell or weight plate, making it highly effective for shoulder integrity and core anti-lateral-flexion strength.

sections.heading: Benefits
sections.content:
- Builds overhead shoulder stability and rotator cuff strength
- Develops anti-lateral-flexion and anti-rotation core control
- Reinforces tall, stacked posture under offset load
- Improves scapular and thoracic positioning
- Highly transferable to overhead pressing and Turkish get-ups
- Strengthens grip and forearm endurance
- Excellent low-impact conditioning tool

sections.heading: Muscles Worked
sections.content:
Primary: Deltoids, Trapezius, Core (Obliques, Rectus Abdominis)

Secondary: Rotator Cuff, Triceps, Forearms, Glutes, Quadriceps

sections.heading: Starting Position
sections.content:
1. Select a kettlebell and stand next to it with feet shoulder-width apart.
2. Squat down to pick up the kettlebell with one hand, gripping the handle firmly.
3. Clean the kettlebell to the rack position at shoulder height.
4. Brace your core and pack your shoulder down.

sections.heading: Execution
sections.content:
1. Press the kettlebell overhead until the arm is fully extended.
2. Keep the wrist straight and the bell stacked over the shoulder, hip, and ankle.
3. Engage core and glutes to maintain a tall, stable posture.
4. Begin walking with controlled, even steps.
5. Keep your gaze forward and avoid leaning or tilting to either side.
6. Walk a predetermined distance or for a set period of time.
7. Carefully lower the kettlebell to the rack, then to the ground, and switch arms to repeat.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- Letting the bell drift forward or behind the head
- Leaning sideways to compensate for the load
- Hyperextending the lower back
- Soft, disengaged shoulder (not packed)
- Bent or collapsed wrist
- Holding breath instead of breathing through bracing
- Walking too fast and losing stacked alignment
- Using a kettlebell too heavy for proper overhead control

sections.heading: Equipment Needed
sections.content:
- Kettlebell of appropriate weight
- Open walking lane (10-30 metres)
- Flat, non-slip flooring
- Optional: Lifting Belt (for heavier loads)
- Optional: Chalk (improves grip)
- Recommended: Flat-soled training shoes

sections.heading: Selecting the Load
sections.content:
1. Start light to learn the overhead position.
2. Choose a weight you can hold overhead with full control.
3. The bell should not waver or pull you sideways.
4. Increase load only when posture stays tall and stacked.
5. Heavier kettlebells challenge stability; lighter ones build endurance.

sections.heading: Body Setup
sections.content:
1. Feet: Shoulder-width apart, toes forward.
2. Hips: Stacked under shoulders, glutes engaged.
3. Core: Braced before pressing the bell overhead.
4. Shoulder: Packed down, away from the ear.
5. Elbow: Fully extended and locked.
6. Wrist: Straight, knuckles toward the ceiling.
7. Gaze: Forward, head neutral.

sections.heading: Similar Exercises
sections.content:
- Waiters Carry: Same overhead pattern with weight plate or dumbbell
- Kettlebell Carry (Rack): Loaded carry with bell in rack position
- Farmers Walk: Bilateral carry at sides for grip and posture
- Suitcase Carry: Single-arm side carry for anti-lateral-flexion
- Bottoms-Up Kettlebell Carry: Rack carry with bell inverted
- Turkish Get-Up: Full overhead stability and mobility drill

sections.heading: Overhead Carry Variations
sections.content:
Single-Arm Overhead Carry: Standard offset load variation
Double Overhead Carry: Two kettlebells held overhead
Mixed Carry: One overhead, one in rack or at side
Bottoms-Up Overhead Carry: Bell inverted for grip and stability
Lunge Overhead Carry: Adds lower-body challenge
Overhead Carry to Press: Combine carry with pressing reps

sections.heading: If You Have Limitations
sections.content:
Shoulder Mobility Issues: Work on thoracic and shoulder mobility first
Rotator Cuff Pain: Reduce load or substitute with rack carry
Lower Back Issues: Avoid hyperextension; reduce distance and load
Grip Issues: Use chalk or shorter sets
No Kettlebell: Use a dumbbell or weight plate (Waiters Carry)
Beginner: Start with a very light bell and short distances to learn position
